{"filepath":"homeowner_explainer.md","content":"# Air‑Source Heat Pumps — A short explainer for UK homeowners

Date: 06 September 2026
Source: based on research_findings.md (Research Specialist, AI)

This short guide explains, in plain English, what an air‑source heat pump (ASHP) is, who it suits, typical costs and running‑cost examples using figures from the research, how to get quotes, and where to find grants. At the end is a one‑page actionable checklist you can use when you start getting quotes.

---

## Plain‑language overview: what is an air‑source heat pump?
- An air‑source heat pump (ASHP) is an electrically powered heating system that extracts heat from the outside air and uses it to heat your home and hot water.
- It is not a boiler: it moves heat rather than burning fuel. Most UK domestic ASHPs are air‑to‑water units that supply your central‑heating system and a hot‑water cylinder.
- ASHPs work best with lower flow temperatures (35–55°C) so they are commonly paired with underfloor heating or larger radiators and with well‑insulated homes.

Callout tip: An ASHP gives multiple kWh of heat for every 1 kWh of electricity used — this is why they can be more efficient than direct electric heating.

---

## Key benefits
- Low operating carbon (especially when the electricity grid or your tariff is low‑carbon or if you have solar PV).
- High efficiency: modern ASHPs typically have seasonal performance (SCOP) in the research range of about 2.8–3.8 (i.e. ~2.8–3.8 kWh heat per kWh electricity).
- No on‑site combustion: no flue and reduced safety/risk concerns compared to oil or LPG boilers.
- Eligible for UK government support (see Grants section).
- Can reduce emissions immediately and — in many homes — lower bills compared with electric resistance heating.

## Key limitations and what to watch for
- Upfront cost: research shows typical installed prices in the UK commonly range from around £6,000 to £15,000 (varies with house type, system complexity and radiator/upgrades needed).
- Performance falls at very low outdoor temperatures (instantaneous COP drops in cold snaps), although seasonal performance (SCOP) captures typical yearly behaviour.
- Works best with good insulation and lower‑temperature distribution. Older, poorly insulated homes or homes with small radiators may need extra insulation or radiator upgrades to get comfortable and efficient performance.
- Noise and siting: the outdoor unit contains a fan and compressor — siting and noise reduction need careful consideration to avoid nuisance to you and neighbours.
- Space: you’ll normally need room for an outdoor unit and a hot‑water cylinder or thermal store inside.

Callout tip: If you have a mains gas connection and a modern gas boiler, fuel bill savings are less certain and depend on electricity price, system performance and your home's insulation.

---

## Typical costs and running‑cost examples (useful figures from the research)
From the research:
- Typical installed cost (UK, modern domestic ASHP): ~£6,000–£15,000 depending on home and complexity.
- Public grant example: the Boiler Upgrade Scheme (BUS) has reduced homeowner net cost for eligible installs by up to about £7,500 (check current scheme rules for eligibility and amounts).
- Typical seasonal performance (SCOP): commonly about 2.8–3.8 for modern ASHPs in UK conditions.

Worked examples (simple, illustrative). These use the research SCOP range and a clear, repeatable method so you can change price and demand numbers to match your situation.

Assumptions you can change: annual heat demand (kWh/yr), chosen SCOP, electricity price (pence/kWh).

Example 1 — Well‑insulated semi or small detached (annual heat demand 8,000 kWh)
- If SCOP = 3.3 (mid‑range from the research): electricity used ≈ 8,000 / 3.3 = 2,424 kWh/yr.
- At an electricity price of 30p/kWh: annual running cost ≈ 2,424 × £0.30 = £727/yr.

Example 2 — Typical (average) home (annual heat demand 12,000 kWh)
- If SCOP = 3.0: electricity used ≈ 12,000 / 3.0 = 4,000 kWh/yr.
- At 30p/kWh: running cost ≈ 4,000 × £0.30 = £1,200/yr.

Example 3 — Larger/poorly insulated older home (annual heat demand 18,000 kWh)
- If SCOP = 2.8 (lower‑end researched seasonal performance): electricity used ≈ 18,000 / 2.8 = 6,429 kWh/yr.
- At 30p/kWh: running cost ≈ 6,429 × £0.30 = £1,929/yr.

Notes on these examples:
- You should replace the electricity price with your own tariff (some suppliers offer specific heat‑pump tariffs or time‑of‑use deals that lower costs).
- The research emphasises that running‑cost comparisons versus gas depend strongly on your current gas price, pump SCOP, and whether radiator/upgrades were required. Installers should provide predicted seasonal performance and an estimated annual electricity use for your home.

Callout tip: Ask each installer to show the predicted annual electricity consumption (kWh/yr) and the assumed SCOP used — this makes quotes easy to compare.

---

## Simple suitability checklist (quick yes/no guide)
- Home type: detached, semi‑detached and terraced houses can all use ASHPs. Smaller well‑insulated homes tend to be cheaper to run. Older large uninsulated homes are less suitable unless major fabric upgrades are done.
- Insulation / fabric: Do you have good loft and wall insulation and double glazing? (EPC C or better is a useful target.) If not, consider insulating before or alongside an ASHP.
- Heating distribution: Do you have underfloor heating or large radiators, or space to install them? If radiators are small, you may need upsized radiators or underfloor heating for comfort and efficiency.
- Outdoor space: Is there a place for an outdoor unit with at least a metre of clearance and good airflow, away from neighbours’ bedroom windows? (Check planning/listed‑building constraints.)
- Noise: Can you site the outdoor unit so it won’t cause nuisance? Ask installers for the unit’s sound power level and predicted sound level at the neighbour boundary.
- Electricity supply: Is your mains supply adequate, or will a supply upgrade be required? Larger systems or hybrid setups may need an electrical upgrade; your installer can advise and liaise with your DNO.

If you answered “no” to several items above, get an independent assessment or ask installers how much building/fabric work they recommend before installing an ASHP.

---

## Steps to get quotes and select an MCS‑certified installer
1. Gather basic info: current heating type, age of house, floor area, EPC rating (if available), and recent heating bills.
2. Ask for at least 3 written quotes from MCS‑certified installers (MCS = Microgeneration Certification Scheme) or equivalent accredited companies. MCS certification is required for many grants and provides quality assurance.
3. For each quote, ask the installer to supply:
   - A room‑by‑room heat‑loss calculation or clear explanation of how sizing was done.
   - The model(s) proposed and their manufacturer SCOP/COP figures and declared sound levels (dB). Request predicted seasonal performance for your house (kWh/yr) and the assumptions used.
   - Details of radiator or underfloor heating changes required (if any) and the extra cost of these upgrades.
   - An itemised price (equipment, installation, electrical upgrades, cylinder, commissioning, warranty and annual service cost estimate).
   - Warranty length and what it covers (compressor, parts, labour), and recommended servicing schedule.
   - References or recent local installations you can check.
4. Compare quotes on consistent assumptions (same heat‑loss data and SCOP assumptions). Don’t pick only on headline price; consider predicted electricity use, warranty and installer reputation.
5. Check the installer’s MCS number on the MCS register and ask if they are registered to process the Boiler Upgrade Scheme (if you want to use it).
6. Before you sign: confirm who will handle the BUS voucher/grant application and what planning/building control sign‑off is needed.

Callout tip: Get the predicted annual kWh and the SCOP in writing from each installer — this is the single most useful figure for comparing running costs.

---

## Available UK grants and how to apply (short overview)
Note: grant schemes change. Always check the official GOV.UK pages or ask installers for up‑to‑date advice.

- Boiler Upgrade Scheme (BUS): a voucher scheme that has been used to reduce homeowner net costs (research notes typical contribution up to ~£7,500). Installers often apply on your behalf; confirm eligibility, voucher value and conditions with the installer or the BUS portal.
- ECO and local authority schemes: Energy Company Obligation (ECO) and local grants can help low‑income or vulnerable households pay for energy‑efficiency and heating upgrades. Availability and eligibility vary by region.
- Local/Devolved government grants: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland run different local schemes at times — check your devolved government and council pages.

How to apply: in most cases, your chosen MCS‑certified installer will register or submit the application for the BUS or other supplier‑led grants as part of the installation process. Confirm who does the application and what paperwork you must provide.

Callout tip: Don’t assume a cheap installer will handle grants correctly — confirm that the installer is familiar with the BUS and any other scheme you intend to use.

---

## Short FAQ (practical answers)
Q: Will an ASHP save me money compared to a gas boiler?
A: Sometimes — it depends on your current boiler efficiency, electricity price, the ASHP’s real seasonal COP (SCOP), and how much insulation/radiator work is needed. Ask installers for an estimated annual electricity use and compare that to your current annual fuel cost.

Q: How noisy are ASHPs?
A: Modern units are much quieter than older models, but they still produce fan and compressor noise. Ask for sound power/pressure figures (dB) and a predicted level at the neighbour boundary or nearest bedroom. Good siting and acoustic screening helps.

Q: How long do ASHPs last and what maintenance is required?
A: Typical lifetime is 15–20 years with proper maintenance. Annual or biennial servicing is recommended; installers can provide service contracts. Keep the outdoor unit clear of debris and vegetation.

Q: Do I need planning permission?
A: Usually not for a domestic ASHP, but rules differ for listed buildings or conservation areas. Check with your local planning authority.

Q: Can I use solar PV with an ASHP?
A: Yes — pairing PV with an ASHP reduces grid electricity use and running costs. Consider battery storage or smart controls to maximise self‑consumption.

---

## One‑page ACTION checklist (use when you start gathering quotes)
- [ ] Check your EPC (if you have one) and note current heating fuel, annual heating kWh if known.
- [ ] Decide budget range and whether you want to use the Boiler Upgrade Scheme (confirm eligibility).
- [ ] Shortlist 3 MCS‑certified installers and request written quotes.
- For each quote, request and keep in writing:
  - [ ] Room‑by‑room heat‑loss calculation or clear sizing report.
  - [ ] Proposed model(s) and declared SCOP/COP and sound level (dB).
  - [ ] Predicted annual heat provided (kWh/yr) and predicted electricity use (kWh/yr).
  - [ ] Exact itemised cost for equipment, installation, radiator/upgrades, electrical works and commissioning.
  - [ ] Warranty details and recommended service schedule + cost.
  - [ ] Who will apply for BUS/other grants (installer or you?).
- [ ] Compare predicted annual electricity use and costs using your electricity tariff (or ask installers to show costs using your tariff).
- [ ] Check MCS registration of chosen installer and ask for references.
- [ ] Confirm planning/building control requirements and who will handle them.
- [ ] Book installation date and agree a snagging/commissioning checklist and handover documentation.

Quick negotiating tip: ask installers to show lifecycle costs (capital + 10 years running) so you can compare long‑term value, not just the upfront price.

---

Further reading and references
- Full research file used to prepare this guide: research_findings.md (same folder)
- Energy Saving Trust — in‑depth guide to heat pumps (UK): https://energysavingtrust.org.uk/advice/in-depth-guide-to-heat-pumps
- GOV.UK — Heat pumps explained and Boiler Upgrade Scheme: https://www.gov.uk/search/news-and-communications?keywords=Boiler%20Upgrade%20Scheme
- National Grid — how do heat pumps work: https://www.nationalgrid.com/stories/energy-explained/how-do-heat-pumps-work

Final tip: use the checklist above and insist on predicted annual kWh and the SCOP value in every written quote — that makes like‑for‑like comparison straightforward.

---

Prepared from: research_findings.md — "Air‑Source Heat Pumps (ASHP) — UK‑focused research findings" (06 Sep 2026).
